He was working as Time Keeper , Se cre ment Assistant and on account of his negligence he committed an act of misconduct punishable under Rule 3 ( 1 )( i ) of the Central Civil Services ( Conduct ) Rules 1966 . On enquiry by the Inquiry Officer , it was found that the respondent had not been able to prove his innocence or guilt beyond reasonable doubt . In view of the findings recorded by the En qu iring Authority , the disciplinary authority imposed penalty of removal from service upon him . An appeal preferred by the respondent before the Appellate Authority failed . The Tribunal set aside the order of punishment and directed reinstatement with all consequential benefits . Hence this appeal by special leave . The petitioners are employed by the respondent Corporation as daily rated workmen . They were paid a sti pend of Rs . 50 per day for doing work in the construction industry . In addition to this , they also received payment from the Corporation under Exhibit P . 2 . The petitioners claim that their services were being treated as regular employees and therefore entitled to be paid wages at par with other workers . The Industrial Tribunal held that the petitioners were not entitled to any minimum wages prescribed by the Government for similar work . On appeal , it was confirmed by the Industrial Court but dismissed . Hence the writ petition . Dismis sing the petition , ^ HELD : 1 . The primary object of the Corporation is to ensure quality of work which is essential for the benefit of the public . It is an obligation of the State to provide adequate employment opportunities to its employees . [ 227 C ] 2 . ( i ) The nature of work undertaken by the Corporation must be such that it can properly meet the requirements of the job . The work performed may be so heavy or otherwise than as would render the same service more useful . But the question whether the work done by the concerned workman should be taken into account while calculating his monthly wages payable to him depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case . [ 228 E F ] ( ii ) The fact that the petitioner had been working as a car p enters does not mean that he was not given the status of a permanent employee . He was merely a casual worker who worked on a temporary basis . His work was only incidental to the main purpose of the corporation . Therefore , the principle of " equal pay for equal work " cannot be applied to the present case . The petitioner ' s claim for regularisation has to be rejected because there is no evidence to show that the work performed by the petitioner was inferior to the work carried out by the respondents . The appellant , a Hindu widow of the late Sad agopal achar and his two daughters , filed a suit for possession against the respondent ' s husband on the ground that he had executed a will in favour of Sad agopal an . The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it holding that the said will was not proved as required by section 63 of the Indian Succession Act , 1925 . In appeal to this Court , HELD : ( 1 ) It is well settled that where there is no specific provision in the will for proving a document or other evidence , the onus lies on the party who seeks its production to prove the same . [ 10 31 B ] ( 2 ) The burden of proof is always on the person who asserts the existence of a particular fact and if he fails to do so , then the one who asserts it must discharge the burden . Where the defendant sets up a case of dis proof , the burden is on him who sets up such a case . [ 1032 E F ] ( 3 ) If the plaintiff alleges a case which is inconsistent with any part of the claim made in the plaint , the court has to presume that the defendant had adopted the stand taken by him in his written statement . But when the defendant pleads that the plaintiff was not willing to take back the properties from the plaintiff , the plaintiff may adduce evidence to show that the adoption took place during the lifetime of the last holder of the property . [ 1033 C D ] ( 4 ) The presumption under section 114 of the Evidence Act applies only to cases where the parties are dead and the plaintiff does not have a strong prima facie case . The question whether the plaintiff has discharged the initial burden of proving that the will was genuine depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case . When the plaintiff claims the property as his absolute owner , he cannot fail to discharge the initial onus placed on him by section 68 of the Act . [ 1034 G H ; 10 35 A ] ( 5 ) The onus of proving the will rests on the prop ounder and the onus shifts on the defendant to establish that the testator did not know the contents of the will . The appellants are manufacturers of electrical apparatus and parts thereof . They were paying duty on the basis that they had been using electric ally for the purpose of producing electricity , which was not a dutiable item under entry No . 4 . The question arose whether the goods manufactured by them would be covered by entry 6 or 7 ( b ) of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act 1957 . Held , that the expression " accessories " in Entry No . 6 meant only those items which were specifically included therein but did not include such items as were used in the manufacture of electric ally consumed power ful light . It is true that the word ' access ory ' has not been defined in the Act ; it may mean any part of an electric system capable of being used to supply energy to the public . But there can be no doubt that the words " parts thereof " have been used in connection with the production of electric energy . The use of these words in the context must necessarily refer to the whole business of the manufacturer .

The petitioners in these petitions are lessees of minor minerals . They were granted quarrying leases for a period of one year from the date of their lease , and they paid royalty at the rate of 50 paise per ton ne of sand extracted by them . In respect of the first petitioner , who was also an applicant before the High Court , the State Government issued a notification under section 3 ( 1 ) of the Act fixing the maximum limit of royalty payable to be collected by persons belonging to the weaker sections of society . On appeal , the Supreme Court held that the power conferred on the State Legislature is not un guided or arbitrary but must be exercised reasonably having regard to the object which it seeks to achieve . It further observed : " The power conferred upon the State Governments to grant permits to the private ent re prene urs to carry on mining operations in certain areas is not an un controlled discretion . There is no inherent right in any person to explo it his mineral as against others . The State has the power to regulate the grant of such permits to others according to their needs and exigencies . But there can be no doubt that the exercise of this power is subject to the restrictions placed by article 47 of the Constitution ." Dismis sing the writ petitions , ^ HELD : 1 . The power to make rules fixing the minimum rates of royalty cannot be said to be an arbitrary power . [ 10 31 B ] 2 . The rule making authority had the power under section 15 of the Mines & Minerals ( Regulation & Development ) Act 1957 to prescribe the manner in which the fee may be levied . This power could be exercised only after consulting the State Advisory Committee constituted under section 4 of the A . P . Minor Mineral Concession Rules 1966 . The powers so conferred have been delegated to the State Govt . by virtue of section 15 read with section 3 of the 1957 Act . [ 1032 C D ] 3 . Section 15 of 1957 Act provides that the Central Government may fix the maximum amount of royalty which may be charged by a licensee in respect of any land in the State . The proviso to section 15 makes it clear that the maximum shall not exceed Rs . 25 / per hectare of the area of every mine where the aggregate of the several minerals exceeds five thousand tonnes . The appellant was elected to the office of trustee in a temple . He filed an application for election under section 5 ( 1 ) of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act , 1951 before the Deputy Commissioner who held that the trustees hip of the temple had been duly registered by the Assistant Collector on January 6 , 1955 . The appellant contended that he was entitled to be declared as hereditary trustee within the meaning of section 6 ( 9 ) of Act 19 of 1951 because his right to manage the affairs of the trust did not come to an end after the death of one of the trustees . Held : ( i ) A person is entitled to succeed to the property of another if there is no other legal impediment ; ( ii ) In order to constitute a successor , it must be shown that the original owner or manager has left any property with him which may have been acquired by succession by inheritance or dev olution from the last male holder , provided that such transferee or successor holds the property only as a limited owner . ( iii ) Section 6 ( 2 ) of Madras Act I of 1951 does not apply to the present case since the respondent ' s claim to the post of trustee was based upon the terms of the deed of settlement executed between the parties . It was not necessary for the purposes of this appeal to establish that the deed was not a mere transfer but a mere act of management .

In respect of the work done after December 1 , 1949 , the real isations were to be divided amongst them as provided in that sub section . For the five assessment years 1950 51 to 1951 52 , the appellants filed returns showing income from various sources including interest paid by them to the firm during those years . The Income tax Officer held that the amounts received by the appellants during the relevant previous year were not taxable as income of the firm but only as representing the assets of the deceased and therefore the amount was liable to be taxed as such . On appeal , the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the ITO but reduced it to Rs . 32 , 523 / and also set aside the penalty imposed upon the appellants . The appellant was a post office clerk in the District Post Office . He had been posted at a station where he was posted for about two months and then to his father ' s house . On May 12 , 1956 , when the Sub Inspector of Police , Bulandsha hr , came there , he found that the appellant had kept certain articles with him on his table and that they were stolen by some unknown person from his house . The Sub Inspector suspected that the ornaments which belonged to the father might have been stolen by somebody else but it was not known as to who had stolen them or how many of those articles were stolen . The appellant denied having ever sold any of these articles to the complainant respondent No . 2 . The case against him was therefore , split up into three distinct charges one under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act 1898 ( VI of 1898 ) and another under section 55 of the , Indian Post Offices Act 1898 . The trial court acquitted the appellant holding that the prosecution failed to prove that the articles seized from the house in question belonged to him . In appeal to the High Court , the State contended that the evidence did not establish that the article seized from his possession was either in the exclusive possession of the appellant or that it belonged to his mother and that the presumption arising under section 54 of the Act could be drawn only if the articles were in their exclusive possession . Held : ( i ) The onus is on the prosecution to prove all the ingredients of an offence under section 7 of the Prevention of Corruption Act , 1947 . The appellant was convicted for contempt of court . He filed a complaint against the respondent , who had been served with a notice under section 2 ( c ) of the Contempt of Courts Act , 1971 and also to an application made by him before the Ny aya Panchayat on December 20 , 1963 alleging that he had disobey ed order dated October 11 , 1963 passed by the Ny ay Panchayat in respect of certain applications submitted by him to the Ny ayal Panchayat . On November 28 , 1963 , the Ny ya Panchayat issued a notice calling upon the respondent to appear at his residence on January 29 , 1964 . The respondent appeared before the Court on February 12 , 1964 but did not appear . The Ny aya panchayat sent a report to the police stating therein that the respondent had committed criminal contempt of the court . The Police Inspector went to the house of the respondent and found him guilty of contempt of Court . The Judicial Magistrate directed the respondent ' s presence in the court on March 1 , 1964 , and ordered that the proceedings be dropped . The matter was taken up by the S . D . M ., who took over charge as Executive Officer of the Panchayat . A copy of the order was forwarded to the respondent . The S . P . after taking into consideration the evidence recorded during investigation , came to the conclusion that there was no prima facie case made out against the accused persons . Accordingly , the S , D . J . dismissed the petition . In revision , the High Court held that the allegations were vague and indefinite and that they could not be said to have been proved beyond reasonable doubt . Allow ing the appeal , ^ HELD : The High Court rightly set aside the order of the S Magistrate and restored the proceeding to its original file . [ 10 31 B ]

He appealed to the High Court against his conviction and sentence but failed . The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentences passed on him . In appeal to this Court it was contended that ( 1 ) there was no evidence in support of the prosecution case which could justify an inference that the appellant had committed the murder ; ( 2 ) the circumstances relied upon by the trial court were not such as would lead to the only conclusion that the accused alone knew what he did with the deceased and therefore the presumption arising under section 106 of the Evidence Act could not be made use of . HELD : ( i ) There is nothing in the statement of the appellant recorded by the police officer where he said that he had seen the dead body of Sheo Swarup at night or that he saw the dead man lying near a tree while going towards the Police Station . [ 10 31 E ] ( ii ) The fact that the dead person was found lying near the well of one Mah mood after the incident clearly shows that the story about the murder must have been made out . It cannot be said that the circumstance relied upon was so improbable as to give rise to a reasonable doubt regarding the guilt of the accused . [ 11 31 B D ] ( iii ) The conduct of the deceased immediately after the occurrence showed that she was not in a position to tell the truth when she went to the Police station and reported the matter to her brother who was present at the Police Post . She also stated that she had told the appellant ' s brother that he should go to the village and report the matter . But the explanation given by the appellant was that she did not know how to proceed to the police station and report dictated by the deceased . [ 32 G H ] ( iv ) The evidence led by the prosecution was sufficient to prove that the deceased was murdered before she left the house and that the evidence adduced by the defence was sufficient enough to establish that the murder took place inside the house of the wife of the witness . The petitioners , who were elected as Councill ors of the Municipal Corporation in the month of December 1978 filed their nomination papers for election to the Municipal Committee . On scrutiny they were found eligible and qualified to contest the elections . They challenged the validity of the election on various grounds including that there was a violation of the provisions of Section 14 ( 1 ) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act 1956 which required that every candidate at an election should be qualified for election as Councillor subject to any qualification prescribed by or under the Act . It was also alleged that the result of the elections had been materially affected because the respondent No . 2 , the Collector of Raipur , issued a public notice dated October 21 , 1978 inviting objections from all persons whose names had not been included in the electoral roll of the Municipality . The petitioner ' s case was that he had submitted his nomination paper after the expiry of the period specified in section 15 ( 3 ) of M . P . Municipalities Act , 1961 and therefore it was incumbent upon him to have made the said application within the time stipulated therein . He further contended that since no objection had been raised against the publication of the draft electoral rolls in accordance with Rule 4 ( 1 ), the election petition could not be dismissed on the ground of delay alone . The High Court rejected this contention holding that the question whether the Returning Officer had given sufficient time to the petitioners to make the nominations is one of discretion and if the Returning officer did not give them reasonable time , the election would be set aside . In appeal to this Court , HELD : ( i ) The words " shall ordinarily be affixed on the Notice " in sub rule ( 1 )( b ) of Rule 4 are mandatory and must be complied with before the date fixed for filing the nomination papers . [ 203 E ] ( ii ) The word " shall " used in sub clause ( b ) does not mean " may ". The use of the word " may " in the context means " shall ". The requirement of complying with the requirements of the rules cannot be dispensed with in order to enable the Returning Officers to complete the process of election but only when the time has expired without making such compliance . [ 204 F G ] ( iii ) The expression " shall be allowed to affix " is capable of meaning " shall ", and unless the context requires otherwise , the same meaning cannot be assigned to it . The appellant company was a public limited company . It had been incorporated in the year 1956 and it was registered under the Indian Companies Act , 1913 . In its balance sheet for the year ending March 31 , 1953 , there were certain items of property which were liable to be included as assets of the company . On January 30 , 1955 , the Registrar of Companies issued a notice calling upon the appellant company to furnish particulars relating to the shares held by them on April 1 , 1954 , and also to show cause why they should not be prosecuted under section 134 ( 4 ) of the Companies Act . The appellant filed an application before the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the said notices . The High Court dismissed the petition holding that no case was made out against the appellant for the contravention of the provisions of sections 76 and 133 of the Act . Hence this appeal . Held : ( i ) The question whether a person charged with an offence can be said to have committed an offence under section 132 or under section 133 of , is one of degree and extent of liability of the directors in respect of the shares acquired by them from the company ; but if the answer to the first part of section 26 is in the affirmative , then only the director could be prosecuted . But where the director has himself taken action under section 131 of the English Act , he cannot be convicted under section 137 of the Indian Penal Code because the director ' s act does not amount to his being in charge of the affairs of the Company .

The appellant , a pro pr itor of the West Bengal Special Courts Ordinance , 1949 , was convicted and sentenced to varying terms of im prison ments by the High Court . He filed an appeal against his conviction and sentence before this Court but that appeal was dismissed in limine on the ground that it was not properly constituted . In view of the decision of this Court in Rao Shiv Bahadur Singh vs State of Vind hya Pradesh ( 1 ), which is also a case relating to the West Pradesh Special Courts Act , 1950 , ి section 3 of the said Act has been amended so as to provide for the speed ier trial of certain offences alleged to have been committed by persons accused of heinous crimes called upon to answer for their lives and liber ties . It is true that under article 14 , no person can be prosecuted or punished for anything done by him in good faith ; yet there are cases where the statute itself provides for a minimum punishment of imprisonment for life and fine only . The question whether the procedure prescribed by the Ordinance should be followed or not would depend on the facts of each case . If the statute prescribes a particular procedure , then the procedure must be such as substantially imposes the same rule of fairness and reasonableness .

The appellant was a Specialist Grade II in the Central Health Service . The appellant , a partnership firm , was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1960 61 . In its return filed under section 139 of the Income Tax Act 1961 , it claimed that in respect of certain assessment years , there were no " good and sufficient reasons " for the assessee ' s failure to file his return within time as required by section 151 ( 2 ) of the Act . On appeal , the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the notice issued under section 148 was invalid because : ( i ) the assessee did not submit the return within the prescribed period ; ( ii ) the return submitted by him was incomplete and therefore could not be entertained ; and ( iii ) the assessment proceedings were barred by limitation . The High Court dismissed the petition . The appellant was a partnership firm carrying on business as a limited company with effect from November 13 , 1947 . On February 7 , 1948 , the two brothers entered into an agreement for sale of their share holdings in the appellant ' s family and agreed to sell their shares to the appellant at certain rates . In pursuance of that agreement they paid Rs . 1 , 000 by way of advance but did not pay any further amount . They were however , asked to make good the balance of the consideration within 15 days failing which the appellant would be entitled to get interest @ 12 % per annum on the sum due till the date of payment . The appellant claimed relief under section 25 ( 4 ) of the Income tax Act , 1922 , read with section 26 ( 2 ) of that Act . The Tribunal held that there had been a succession between the three brothers and therefore it could not be said that there was a succession within the meaning of section 26 . Held : ( i ) It is well settled that if one who owns property or assets , dies leaving behind his widow and children , then only the other person who has acquired a right to succeed to the estate of the deceased can claim relief under Section 25 ( 2 ). But where the deceased died without having any issue , he being the sole heir of the last owner , the question whether the death took place during the life time of the exec utor or after his death does not arise . ( ii ) Where a person dies leaving no legal heir except the real surviving member of the joint family , the court will have regard to the fact whether the deceased left him surviving as a result of the death of the person succeeding to the property of the adop tive father . If the deceased leaves no heir capable of taking care of the properties of the natural father , such as a manager , trustee etc ., the Court may hold that the adopted son was alive when the suit was filed .

The appellant , a Hindu widow of the deceased , was the sole surviving member of her husband ' s family . She had two sons and three daughters who were married in 1947 . In 1956 she died leaving behind her son , his wife and children as his heirs . On November 6 , 1962 , the appellant filed an application under section 4 of the Bombay Tenancy Act for partition of the joint family properties contending that he was entitled to 1 / 4th share in the joint property which was allotted to him by the respondent . The trial court dismissed the application holding that the appellant was not entitled to any share in these properties because there was no partition between himself and his two sons . The High Court held that since the appellant had acquired only one half share in all the joint properties , it could not be said that he had acquired another half share therein . Allow ing the appeal , ^ HELD : ( i ) The view taken by the Bombay High Court is correct . [ 591 E ] ( ii ) Section 3 of the Hindu Women ' s Right to Property Act , 1937 , provides that where a Hindu dies int estate , his interest in the property shall devol ve according to the provisions of this Chapter on the happening of such event . Section 5 of the Act deals with dev olution of interest in coparcen ary property . It says that " Where a Hindu int estate has vested in an absolute owner or full owner , as the case may be , under section 14 , then , the interest of the female Hindu in the Mit aksh ara coparcen ary governed by the Day abh aga School of Hindu Law prevailing at the time of her death shall be deemed to have been transferred to the share of the male Hindu in that property ." [ 592 G H ; 593 A B ] ( iii ) The expression " Hindu W oman " used in section 2 ( 15 ) means a person who acquires by birth an interest in a joint family property . Therefore , if a Hindu alien ee takes a daughter ' s share in certain properties belonging to her father , she becomes entitled to a share in those properties also . If she transfers her share in them , she would get only a life interest in those items . That being so , the transfer of the entire interest in favour of the appellant must be treated as having been made after the coming into force of the Amendment Act , 1929 . [ 594 C D ] ( iv ) The words " Hindu Wid ow " in section 3 of Act XXX II of 1959 are wide enough to include fem al es who acquire by inheritance or succession

The appellant was a member of the Bar Association . He had come to Court on February 20 , 1975 and filed an application for contempt against the respondent alleging that he had taken certain documents from his clients in order to help them in the election petition filed by him . The High Court dismissed the application holding that it did not lie under section 2 ( c ) of the Contempt of Courts Act , 1971 as there was no provision in the Act or any other law which authorised the court to take cognizance of the matter . In appeal to this Court , HELD : 1 . It is well settled that if the words used are capable of one construction only then they must be construed according to their plain meaning . [ 247 C ] 2 . The expression " cause of action " means the circumstances existing at the time when the acts complained of were alleged to have been done with the intention of der iving support from legal restrictions imposed by law upon the conduct of the parties . If the allegations made in the letter are such that the Judge could legitimately reach to the conclusion that the facts disclosed by the letters were true , the charge may be held to have not been proved . [ 248 F G ; 249 A B ] 3 . The object of the Act is to punish the guilty and protect the person who has committed breach es of the law . The offence should be such so as to enable the judge to preserve the dignity of the court and to deter persons from acting in furtherance thereof . [ 250 D E ] 4 . The Judges cannot go into the merits of the case unless the same is shown to be frivolous or vexatious . [ 251 H ] 5 . There is nothing wrong in the language of the statute requiring that before taking any action against the judges , the Chief Justice of Punjab and Haryana High Court should give notice to the members of the bar association . [ 252 B ] 6 . The Chief Justice can call the meeting of the State Bar Council and hear the advocates but he cannot act as a representative body . The power conferred on the Chief Jus tices under Article 124 ( 2 ) is not intended to be exercised in a way which would result in the institution of a proceeding which is calculated to interfere with the administration of justice . [ 253 C ] 7 . The Supreme Court Rules require that where a motion for taking action against a Judge is presented to the President for the removal of the Judge , the President shall obtain the opinion of the Attorney General of India . The Constitution does not contemplate that the Chief Minister of Haryana will have to seek the opinion

The appellant was a Hindu undivided family consisting of the two brothers . In 18 37 , the estate was divided between them and the appellant ' s father in 19 17 transferred his interest to the appellant who had been granted a pension by the Government under the law for the time being in force . On the death of the father , the appellant became entitled to receive from the Government an ann uity on the footing that he was the owner of the estate as defined in section 2 ( 4 ) of the Indian Income tax Act , 1922 . The question arose whether the payment made to the respondent was income or not within the meaning of section 10 of the Income Tax Act , 1961 . Held , that the amount received by the appellant as compensation for the acquisition of the right to receive the whole or any part of it could be regarded as a capital receipt . It is immaterial that the payment was made to him out of the proceeds of the property acquired . The fact that the appellant did not have the money would not make any difference because the amount which was paid to him was merely compensation for acquiring the title to the land .

The appellant State Transport Authority , in exercise of its powers under section 63 ( 7 ) of the Motor Vehicles Act , 1939 , issued a notification dated March 30 , 1984 granting permits to the appellants for plying their vehicles on certain routes . The said permit was granted by the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation and an application for grant of such permits was made by the appellants who were applicants before the Tribunal . The appellants challenged the validity of the scheme as being violative of Article 14 of the Constitution of India on the ground that it violated the fundamental right guaranteed to them under article 19 ( 1 )( g ) of Constitution of the India . The High Court held that the provisions of the proviso to section 63 of the Act were not applicable to the applications which had been filed after the date of the publication of the Scheme and therefore they were invalid . In appeal to this Court , HELD : ( i ) The proviso to Section 63 ( 3 ) is valid and does not contraven e any of the rights conferred by Article 19 ( l )( g ). [ 128 D ] ( ii ) The scheme framed by the Central Government under section 68 of the , provides for the manner in which the approval can be given and the conditions subject to which the same may be accorded . It is true that there are no guidelines or rules prescribed for the purpose of giving effect to the scheme but the fact remains that the scheme itself has to be implemented and the persons operating the tourist buses have to be accommodated in the tourist bus . There is nothing in the Act which prevents the appellants from applying for the grant of permits to others similarly situated . [ 129 E F ; 130 A B ] ( iii ) The object of the legislature in enacting the proviso is to ensure that the operators of tourist vehicles should be able to operate their existing stage carriages with all facilities available at their disposal so that the number of permits granted to them would not exceed 25 per cent of the total number of vehicles owned by them . This means that if the number is more than the number specified , then the number will be reduced to less than 25 . That is why the proviso gives power to the Regional Transport Authority to refuse to grant permission to the operator of a particular stage carriage to ply his vehicle without following the procedure laid down in the proviso . [ 131 G H ] ( iv ) The words " other than those mentioned in sub clause ( v ) of clause ( b ) of subsection ( 2 ) of section 63 " mean only temporary permits granted by a Regional Transport authority and not temporary permits .

The appellant was appointed senior jail or as a Superintendent of Police in the State of Saurashtra . He was suspended from service on February 2 , 1954 and he was served with a charge sheet for certain acts of misconduct committed by him during his period of suspension . On March 6 , 1953 , he was suspended and an enquiry was held against him . In due course , the Enquiry Officer submitted his report holding that the charges were proved . The disciplinary authority dismissed the respondent ' s appeal but the High Court allowed the petition filed by the respondent . It was contended before this Court that the order of dismissal passed against the respondent was illegal because it was not based on any evidence ; that the respondent had been acquitted by the criminal court and there was no finding that the departmental inquiry was bad ; that even if the departmental proceedings were invalid , the respondent could be reinstated only after the decision of the Criminal Court in respect of the offences charged against him ; and that since the respondent did not hold any post under Government at the time when the order was made , he could not be deemed to have ceased to hold the office of Superintendent of police . Held : ( 1 ) that the words " civil servant " occurring in section 60 ( 3 ) of the Act mean a person who is employed in connection with the affairs of the Union or of a State and does not include a person whose services are temporarily attached to another department . ( 2 ) That the word " civil servants " in section 61 means persons other than those mentioned therein and includes all officers and servants of a local or other authority within the meaning of article 311 of the Constitution . ( 3 )( i ) A civil servant can be said to hold a civil post within the definition of that expression in section 3 ( 14 ) of Bombay Civil Service Act , 1947 , which is analogous to the Indian Railway Establishment Code . ( ii ) The respondent was a railway employee and therefore entitled to the payment of salary for the period of his absence from duty . ( iii ) The provisions of section 60 of the Bombay Re illy vs R apply to the case of a railway servant who has been dismissed from service and removed from service while he was still in service .

The appellant was granted a lease of the coal mine in 1953 . On June 10 , 19 01 , he applied for a mining lease to one Wal ji Khe ta which had been granted by the Government of India on August 18 , 1941 . Under cl . ( 3 ) of the said rule the lessee was required to pay at least 25 % of the total amount payable as dead rent and royalty . In pursuance of this condition the appellant paid Rs . 1 , 000 per year as dead - rent . Thereafter , the appellant filed an application under r . 14 of the Indian Mines Act , 1923 , praying that the respondent should be directed to vacate the land within three years from the date of its grant . The Assistant Collector held that the appellant ' s claim was barred by limitation but rejected it holding that the respondents were entitled to get possession of the land after they had obtained a lease from the original owner . He also found that there was no evidence to show that the appellants had encroached upon any portion of their coal mines or that the area did not belong to them . Held , that the finding of the courts below that the suit was barred under art . 120 Of the Limitation Act could not be sustained . It is well settled that if a party has committed a breach of contract , his remedy lies elsewhere than a suit . But where the breach of conditions is alleged , the court may refuse to enforce the contract because it is not made out that the breach was so fundamental as to give rise to a triable issue . The mere fact that the plaintiff had notice of the breach would not entitle him to obtain relief under article 226 of the Constitution .

In the meanwhile , when the management decided to dismiss him , the appellant raised an industrial dispute which was referred for adjudication under section 10 ( 1 ) of the Act . The respondent was appointed as the Secretary in the District Sol di er Board of Un na o on 20 . 8 . 1979 and he was appointed on contract basis for a fixed term from 1 . 6 . 1983 to 30 . 8 1985 by an order dated 1st June , 1983 . In his appeal before this Court , it was contended that since the termination of services of the respondent was not based on any misconduct but only because of his unsatisfactory work , there was no question of holding an inquiry into the allegations made against him . The appellant was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life . He appealed to the High Court against his conviction , but the High court dismissed it summarily on the ground that there were no sufficient reasons for interfering with the order of acquittal . In appeal by special leave , HELD : ( 1 ) There is nothing in the evidence which may give any indication that the deceased had been assaulted or murdered by the accused or that he had a reasonable doubt about the veracity of the prosecution case . [ 10 31 B ] ( 2 ) It is not possible to say that the view taken by the Trial Court was unreasonable or perverse . [ 1032 E F ] ( 3 ) The fact that the appellant was seen last with the deceased immediately after the occurrence cannot be a sole ground for rejecting his testimony . [ 1033 C D ] ( 4 ) The conduct of the appellant in not telling the truth when he was examined as a witness before the Sessions Judge would show that he did not have an opportunity to see him earlier at all . If the version given by the appellant ' s mother is believed then she must have told her brother who was present near the house of the accused and asked him why he had gone to sleep . She also stated that she had not heard anyone from the family members of the deceased till they came out of the house . [ 1034 G H ] ( 5 ) The defence witnesses are natural witnesses and their statements should be carefully scrutinised with care and caution because they do not appear to be un truthful . [ 1038 A ] ( 6 ) The trial court has rightly relied upon the statement of the father of the girl , P . W . 1 , who was living with the appellant since long and was closely related to the deceased . The High Court has accepted the evidence of P . Ws . 1 to 3 without any hesitation . [ 1044 B ]

The appellant was a Judge of the Supreme Court and he was charged with an offence under section 5 ( 1 )( e ) read with section 2 of the Prevention of Corruption Act , 1947 . He was tried by the Special Judge for offences punishable under sections 7 and 13 ( 1 ) ( d ) and Section 5 ( 2 ) of the Act . The trial court acquitted him on both counts but convicted him under section 7 of the said Act . On appeal to the High Court it was contended that the provisions of clause ( e ) of sub section ( 1 ), of section 5 of the Code were not applicable in respect of Judges who are public servants within the meaning of section 2 ( c ) of Criminal Law Amendment Act , 1952 . It was also urged that since the Judges of the High Courts are public servant they could be prosecuted only if they had committed criminal misconduct as defined in section 6 ( 1 ). Dismis sing the appeal , ^ HELD : 1 . In view of the definition of ' public servant ' in section 2 , there is no warrant for excluding any person from its purview . [ 10 31 B ] 2 . The expression " public servant " has been used in section 21 of the Indian Penal Code which defines public servant as including every person employed or appointed by a public servant to do any official act whether preliminary or pre t ended , or not , in connection with his affairs . The word ' public ' is not confined to private persons alone . A distinction must be made between the two while appointing a public officer to a post under the Government and the appointment of a dismissed public servant . If the former is held to include a government servant , then even though the latter may have no relationship whatsoever with the public servant , he will continue to hold office until the termination of the proceedings by way of punishment . [ 1032 E F ] 3 . There is nothing in the language of section 6 to indicate that the words " other public servant ", i . e ., " public officer " would refer to a public authority . The use of the words ' includes ' indicates that the legislature intended to exclude some other categories of public servants from the scope of the enactment . [ 1033 C D ] 4 . The object underlying the provision is to prevent frivolous complaints against public servants . But this does not mean that the Legislature did not intend to cover such cases at all . [ 1034 G ] 5 . The appellant , a candidate for election to the West Bengal Legislative Assembly from the Khar gram Murshid abad constituency of West Bengal was declared elected . On August 10 , 1950 , he filed an Election Petition challenging the validity of the election on various grounds . In his petition before the High Court he contended that there were several other candidates who had been declared elected and that those who bore the sur name Saha belonged to a Scheduled Caste . The High Court held that the appellant did not belong to any Scheduled Caste but only to one of the five persons mentioned in item 40 . It also found that the respondent ' s case fell within the four corners of article 16 ( 4 ) of the Constitution . Held : ( i ) that the question whether a person belongs to a scheduled caste or a scheduled tribe is essentially a question of fact ; it cannot be decided by this court under Article 136 of the constitution unless it is shown that the decision is vitiated by mala fides or is based on no evidence . ( ii ) That the Tribunal has jurisdiction to decide questions which are purely academic in nature . The view taken by the Tribunal was correct . The appeal must therefore fail .

The appellant and respondent No . 2 were partners in a partnership firm carrying on business as manufacturers of various products , including pain ts , var nish es , etc ., which was being manufactured by the appellant . In order to carry out this contract they entered into an agreement with the appellant for the supply of certain goods . Under that agreement the appellant agreed to pay Rs . 30 , 000 per month towards the price of the goods supplied at the time of delivery and also to pay interest thereon at 3 % p . a . from the date of payment till the date when the amount became due and payable . On failure to make the payment within the stipulated period the appellant was liable to be prosecuted under section 7 ( 1 ) read with section 13 ( 4 ) of the Prevention of Corruption Act , 1947 . The prosecution case was that the appellant had promised to deliver the goods to the complainant or his partner if he failed to do so . The appellant denied having delivered any goods to him . He pleaded that there was no privity of contract between him and the complainant and that the transaction was not one of sale but of bail ment . Held : ( i ) It is well settled that where two views are possible , the court should lean in favour of the accused rather than against the prosecution . Where it appears that the view taken by the trial judge is reasonable and plausible , it is open to the appellate court to interfere with the acquittal even though the other view may not be reasonably possible . But where the trial court has held that the evidence does not show that the accused offered the goods and accepted the goods without protest , then the question arises whether the presumption arising under section 118 can be raised against the accused . If the accused fails to rebut the presumption , the burden would lie on him to prove that the presumption is rebutted . The standard of proof required is that of a criminal trial . Even if the accused pleads guilty , the Court must proceed on the basis that the preponderance of probability is in favour . Of course , the standard of proving beyond reasonable doubt is not applicable to the facts and circumstances of each case .

The appellant , a company registered under the Indian Companies Act , 1956 , was carrying on business of manufacturing and selling ready made garments . In its factory at Bombay it had employed about 10 , 000 employees in its factory . It also used to carry out certain other works such as construction of roads , bridges etc . On January 31 , 1975 the Company issued a notice terminating the services of all the workmen including the appellants who were working in the factory . The dispute related to revision of wage scales by the Company for the years 1974 , 1975 and 1976 respectively . The Tribunal held that the revised wage scale of the employees would be applicable only from July 1 , 1973 when they completed 240 days of service and not from any earlier date . The Company contended before the Industrial Tribunal that the revision of pay scales should be with effect from April 1 , 1972 because the revision was effective from August 1 , 1977 whereas the award was published on December 22 , 1978 . The Union filed an application before the Tribunal claiming that the Tribunal ' s award should be modified so as to bring uniformity in the matter of dearness allowance . The claim was resisted by the appellant contending that since the Company did not choose to amend the Award by adding the words " basic wages ", the revision petition should be dismissed . The High Court allowed the application holding that the amendment was not retrospective but was prospective . Allow ing the appeal , this Court , HELD : ( i ) The question whether the Tribunal could have altered the existing wage scales or not is essentially one of fact depending upon the facts and circumstances of each case . [ 227 E ] ( ii ) The Tribunal has given satisfactory reasons for adopting a different method of computing dearness allowance based on the prevailing wage rates . The said decision cannot be said to be either erroneous or perverse . [ 228 C D ] ( iii ) The scheme of dearness allowances being linked to the cost of living index , there can be no doubt that the dearness allowance which is payable to the employees must be similar to the one paid to the comparable employ ments . [ 229 B C ] ( iv ) The dearness allowance is admissible only if there are two conditions precedent namely , ( i ), that the increase in the rate of dearness Allowance shall be neutral ised by way of addition of neutral isation to the amount of rise in prices ; and ( ii ). If the employer wants to include dearness allowance in the cost price of living Index , he has to give evidence to prove that the rise in the costs of living will be due to the increased cost of production . The appellant , a private limited company , was awarded by the Government of India under an award made in 1947 . In pursuance of that award , the management of the appellant paid its employees certain amounts from time to time as wages for work done by them and also fixed by the award . The respondent filed a suit against the appellant claiming wages at Rs . 2 / per day for the period between April 1 , 1948 , to March 31 , 1949 , on the ground that it had been paid to him without any protest or demur . The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal . On appeal to this Court , HELD : ( i ) The payment of wages is not a condition precedent to the validity of the award ; it is merely a matter of procedure . It does not create a right in favour of the employee which he has acquired before the proceedings are concluded and no question of estoppel can arise . [ 10 75 F ] ( ii ) The fact that the amount payable to the workman was reduced by the appellate tribunal would not make any difference because the order passed by the High court was set aside by the Supreme Court in exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution . [ 1072 B C ] ( iii ) The principle underlying section 2 ( vi ) of the Act cannot be applied to the present case since there was no dispute about the rate of wages prescribed by the Tribunal . [ 1073 G H ] ( iv ) Section 15 of the Payment of Wages Act , 1936 provides that " every employer shall pay to every employee engaged in any scheduled employment during the financial year one month ' s wages ". Therefore , if the wages were revised after the date of the notification of the said section , the wages payable to such workmen could only be those which were actually paid by the employer . If the wages are increased by the subsequent amendment of the definition of wages , then the wages so increased will have to be taken into account for calculating the amount of compensation payable to each employee . [ 1074 A D ] ( v ) The object of the legislature in enacting section 2 of the Industrial Disputes Act is to provide a remedy for the employees who may not be able to get their wages beyond what they might receive earlier than the minimum wage rates prescribed by industrial adjudication . [ 1052 E F ]

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department , Pep su . He was charged with an offence under section 465 of the Indian Penal Code for having received Rs . 51 from the accused as illegal gratification and that he had not done any official duty or acted in excess of his authority . The prosecution case was that on the date when the appellant was put up by the police at the Police Station he had received Rs , 51 from one Ram Singh who was a clerk in the office of the District Magistrate , Patiala , which amount was paid to him by the latter . On the basis of this payment , the appellant ' s explanation was found to be false and therefore prosecuted . Held , that sanction was necessary before cognizance could be taken against the appellant . It is well settled that where a public servant acts malic iously and fraudulently , it is not sufficient that he should have obtained the sanction of the Government . In the present case , the act complained of did not fall within the scope of his duties , but merely because the money was paid into the treasury , and the question whether the act was done in execution of the duty or not would depend upon the facts of each case .

The assessee was a public limited company incorporated in the State of Travancore and it had its registered office in British India . It filed its return for the assessment year 1948 49 , showing an income of Rs . 11 , 872 for the previous years ending June 30 , 1949 , and December 31 , 1949 . In respect of the first two appeals the Appellate Tribunal held that the business loss incurred by the assessee during those years was not liable to be included in the total income of the assessee under section 10 ( 1 ) of the Indian Income tax Act 1922 . On appeal by special leave the appellant contended that the High Court erred in holding that the proviso to section 24 ( 1 )( b ) of Travancore Act did not apply to the case of the second proviso to sub clause ( i ) of section 24 of the Travancore Act as it applied only to cases where the profits or gains were taxable in the hands of the asses se if they arose outside the State . Held : ( 1 ). The proviso to subsection ( 1 ), which is a general provision dealing with computation of agricultural income , applies to all cases falling within the category mentioned therein ; but the proviso does not say that such cases must be deemed to have arisen in any part of the State from which the income has been derived . ( 2 ) The proviso is intended to deal with cases of persons who are resident in the taxable territories and whose income is being computed under the head ' Prof its and gains of business in British Indian States '. Therefore , the words " business in the Indian State " occurring in the proviso do not refer to business in another State . ( 3 ) Section 32 ( 1 ): does not expressly mention the word " business " in the main part of section 10 . But this would make no difference because the proviso refers to business which is carried on in the territory of India . ( 4 ) The Explanation to section 10 of the Act does not refer only to business of the kind referred to in section 10 , namely , the business of banking , and therefore it cannot be said that the legislature intended to exclude business in a foreign country from the operation of the proviso . ( 5 ) The object of the Explanation is to explain the meaning of the expression " business ". If the Legislature wanted to include business in one place in the other then the explanation would have used the words ' business in India ' also . [ 59 E F ] ( 6 ) The fact that the words in the Explanation mean business in different places in the same State will not affect the scope of the Proviso

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1946 as a Private Limited Company . Its head office at Calcutta , which is also a subsidiary of the respondent company , was incorporated on January 1 , 1946 with its registered office at Bombay and it had branches all over India . In September , 1959 an agreement was entered into between the parties for fixing the age of retirement at 60 . Under this agreement the employees were to retire at 55 or 60 years after they attained the age 58 . On December 31 , 1956 the Government of India issued a notification under section 4 ( 2 ) of the Industrial Disputes Act , 1947 , prescribing the age limit of superannuation for workmen employed in any industry in India . This notification was followed by another notification dated May 25 , 1958 , published in the Gazette of India , Part II , Section 3 , sub section ( i ), of that date , providing that no workman shall be retired from service except with the previous approval of the Central Government . By another notification , the Central Govt . fixed the age at 60 as the age for industrial workers who had been working for more than five years before the said date . The Tribunal held that there was nothing in the award to show that the age was fixed at 60 ; but it further held that the question whether the age should be fixed at 55 was not decided by the Tribunal because the evidence showed that the number of persons employed in each case would have been different . It therefore directed that the matter should be remitted to the Tribunal for determining the age . The appellants then filed applications for special leave to appeal against the decision of the Tribunal . Held : ( i ) That the Tribunal had jurisdiction to decide the question of age of superannuation only if it came to the conclusion that the employee concerned must be deemed to have continued in service even after he has put in such length of service as might be necessary to enable him to discharge his duties efficiently . ( ii ) The Tribunal had committed an error in holding that the appellant ' s contention that the respondents were entitled to continue in service till 60 was accepted . ( iii ) The tribunal had erred in law in holding otherwise . [ 59 E F ] ( iv ) There was no basis for the assumption made by the Tribunals that the period during which the appellant could be retained in service after attaining the age Of 58 was merely a formality . The fact that the Tribunal did not consider the effect of the order passed by the Government itself shows that the High Court was not justified in interfering with the order of the Government .

The appellant was convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to five years rigorous imprisonment . He appealed to this Court by special leave against his conviction , but the High Court confirmed the sentence . Allow ing the appeal , ^ HELD : ( 1 ) There is no evidence that the daco its had committed dacoity in any way . It is not possible for this court to come to a conclusion on the basis of the circumstances of each case whether all or any of them were members of an unlawful assembly . [ 10 31 B ] ( 2 ) The fact that the appellant was found with some other persons at the time when he was caught while committing dacoity does not mean that he was one who committed dacoity . In the present case it cannot be said that there was any pre med itation on the part of the appellant to commit robbery . The offence was committed at night by as many as 20 persons including the appellant . [ 1032 C D ] ( 3 ) The appellant ' s conduct shows that he did not take proper care about the place where the stolen property was kept . He could have taken the goods from another person if he was available . But the fact remains that the ornaments which were recovered from him were not belonging to him nor were they seized . Therefore the presumption arising out of the facts mentioned above can only be drawn . [ 1033 E F ] ( 4 ) The courts below rightly held that the charge against the appellant has been proved beyond reasonable doubt . [ 1034 G ]

The petitioners who are the owners of a sugar mill and manufacturing only those thin ners which contain more than one ingredient , were granted a licence to sell such an article . They challenged the vires of Section 5 ( 1 )( d ) on the ground that it is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as they have been discriminated against by the State Government in granting them licences for sale of the same substance . It was contended that the provisions of Rule 2 ( x )( 2 ) of the Rules were discriminatory and arbitrary and therefore violative of Articles 14 and 19 ( 1 ) ( g ) of Constitution . The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that there was no material before the authority to show that the petitioner had any right to carry on the business under the Act or that he could not be said to have violated his fundamental rights . In appeal to this Court , HELD : ( i ) The power conferred upon the Government by Rule 2 of the rules is un guided and un canal ised and cannot be struck down on the plea that the rule violates the fundamental rights guaranteed under Part III of the Con sti t ution . [ 226 E ] ( ii ) The impugned notification and its application to any area would depend on the necessity to declare the substance as poison for the entire country . If the intention of the Government was to prohibit the possession and sale of any essential commodity at a particular place , then the provision contained in sub section ( 2 ) thereof would prevail over the provisions contained in Chapter IV A of the Act . [ 227 B C ] ( iii ) The object of the enactment is to prevent exploitation of the people and to ensure that the common man does not commit any act which may result in injury to others . The purpose of the legislation is to regulate the trade and commerce in intoxic ants . [ 228 D ] ( iv ) The question whether the restrictions imposed by the statute are reasonable or not has to be determined with reference to the nature of the trade or business in which the commodities are sold . The object and scope of the law is to protect the society from the anti social evil . [ 229 F G ]

The assessee , a firm carrying on business at Bombay as importers of yarn and also as agents for the sale proceeds of cotton yarn sold by it to its customers in Bombay , filed returns showing profits from sales made to various parties . In the assessment year 1952 53 , the Income tax Officer disallowed the deduction claimed under section 10 ( 2 ) ( vi ) of the Indian Income Tax Act , 1922 on the ground that the amounts were not received by the assessee in his own name but in the name of his wife and daughter . On appeal , the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the sums were not liable to be deducted as those were paid out of the income of the assessee ' s business . He further found that the amount was not credited into the accounts of the appellant company or any other person except the assessee who had been given credit for payment of interest on loans taken by him . The Tribunal however allowed the claim holding that the sum of Rs . 2 , 68 , 385 / was not an allowable expenditure because no part of the amount could have been debited to the profit and loss account of the respondent firm . The High Court answered the question against the Department . Dismis sing the appeal to this Court , HELD : 1 . It is well settled that if there is some reasonable basis for the conclusion that the money was not sent to the assessee for which he has incurred the liability , then the same must be shown to have been received by him in the ordinary course of his business . [ 423 C D ] 2 . The fact that the moneys were sent to a different concern does not mean that they are received in the usual course of the business of the asses ee . They are received by one concern only when the entire amount is transferred to another concern . If the money is not so transferred to the other concern , it cannot be said that the monies were not sent by the appellant to the Bombay firm in the normal course of its business . There is nothing in the statement of case to show that the funds sent to Bombay firm were not actually received by it in the course of their business . Therefore , the finding with regard to the whole of the consideration received by way of loan from the Bombay Company is correct . [ 424 F G ; 425 A B ] 3 . The principle underlying section 10 of the Income Tax , Act , 1961 is that where the income is chargeable to income tax , the receipt must be received by a person directly in his capacity as agent of the other party . The petitioners , who were the owners of certain lands acquired by the State Government under the Land Acquisition Act for a public purpose , filed petitions in this Court challenging the acquisition proceedings . They also challenged the validity of Section 11 A of the Land Acqu is tion Act on various grounds including that they had not been served with notice and opportunity to file their objections against the proposed acquisition ; that the Special Leave Petitions should be dismissed as having become infructuous since no stay order was granted by any court ; and that the notification making the declaration under section 4 of the Act was invalid because it did not comply with the requirement of sub section ( 2 ) of Section 17 of the said Act . Dismis sing the special leave petitions , HELD : 1 . It is well settled that where the land has been notified under Section 4 of Land Acquisition act , 1894 , the award must be made within two years from the date of publication of the notification under Section 6 of the L . A . Act . [ 10 31 B ] 2 . In view of the fact that the awards have been made within the stipulated time , there can be no doubt that the delay in filing the writ petition or in preferring the appeal would not affect the right of the claimants to get compensation under the provisions of the LA Act . Therefore , the High Court was justified in dismissing the Writ Petition . [ 1032 C D ] 3 . The question whether the delay caused in taking steps to take possession of the lands from the appellants could be taken into consideration while computing the period of limitation does not arise . [ 1033 E F ]

The appellant bank was a banking company . It had been carrying on business in the nature of banking , and its working hours were from January 1 , 1959 to April 30 , 1960 . On March 31 , 1961 the Bank issued a notice under section 33 C ( 2 ) of the Industrial Disputes Act , 1947 , for determining the pay scales of workmen employed in banks which were not governed by the Sas try Award as modified by the Labour Appellate Tribunal decision dated August 26 , 1963 . In the first group of appeals before this Court it was contended that the award did not state any reasons for fixing the pay scale at Rs . 175 but only stated that the employees would be fitted in the new scales of pay provided by the Desai award . Allow ing the appeal , ^ HELD : ( i ) The award is clear and specific . There is no reason why the clerical staff should have been given the higher pay than what they are entitled to under sub cl . ( d ) of cl . 29 of the Sas ty Award . [ 1009 B ] ( ii ) The tribunal has made an error in holding that the revised pay scale of Rs . 182 with effect from January l , 1962 was fixed at Rs , 170 . The High Court erred in taking the view that the original pay scale was Rs . 184 and not Rs . 112 . [ 1010 E G ] ( iii ) The High Courts order is correct and does not suffer from any infirmity . [ 1011 D ] ( iv ) The scheme of dearness allowance is based upon the basic pay in the Sas ri ' s case and there is nothing wrong or illegal in fixing the same at Rs 108 . The minimum pay in that cadre is Rs . 180 . That being so , the maximum pay prescribed by the award cannot be fixed at more than Rs . 108 . [ 1012 A ]

The first appellant , a registered association of small scale industries in the State of Andhra Pradesh , was an Association for the development of small and medium industries . It had been formed by the Government of India under section 3 ( 1 ) of the Industries ( Development & Regulation ) Act , 1951 . The second appellant is a company incorporated under the Companies Act which has its own rules and regulations governing the business of the first appellant . Its membership number is as follows : " A group of persons having interest in large industrial units with more than 50 per cent shares in the capital of the industry would be entitled to participate in the general meetings of such other groups . The members of the group are not permitted to vote on their behalf unless they have made any specific request or request in writing from them ." The appellants were members of one trade union called ' A ' which was affiliated to the Indian Chamber of Commerce . They were also members of another Trade Union called ' B ' which had no voting rights over the affairs of the club . In the year 1965 , the first respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the said order . The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that there was no violation of Article 19 ( 1 )( c ) of Constitution . Hence this appeal . Allow ing the appeal , ^ HELD : 1 . The expression ' unions ', used in the definition clause must be given a broad meaning so as to include within it even those who seek to es p ouse the cause of the labour . The word ' unions ' cannot be construed in a narrow way but must be read as broadly as possible . If the words ' unions , trade unions , business organisations etc . are understood in the sense of a trade union , then the very purpose of the legislation will be defeated . [ 281 G H ; 282 A ] 3 . The provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act , 1947 , provide for the regulation of the conditions of service of employees including terms and conditions of employment of workmen employed therein . The assessee , a partnership firm carrying on business in the name and style of M / s . Ram Prasad & Sons Pvt . Ltd ., filed its returns for the assessment years 1957 58 to 1958 59 under section 10 ( 1 ) of the Income Tax Act , 1961 . In the course of assessment proceedings , it claimed that the assessee had made gift aggreg ating Rs . 67 , 560 / 12 / out of his net wealth of Rs . 50 , 000 by making an investment of Rs , 25 , 000 in the account books . The assessing authority held that the sum of Rs 1 lakh was properly included in the assessee ' s net wealth as income from property . On appeal , the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the assessing authority but allowed the appeal holding that the amount of Rs 2 lakhs received by the assessee as gift tax was not liable to be taxed as capital gains . The Tribunal further held that since the assessee did not make any gift of Rs 50 , 00 , 000 to his wife and daughter , he could not be said to have acted as a trustee or manager of the assessee company . The High Court answered the question in favour of the Revenue and against the assessee . Hence this appeal by special leave . Allow ing the appeal , ^ HELD : 1 . A gift may be regarded as a transfer of property within the meaning of section 10 of the Indian Income Tax , 1922 . [ 11 C ] 2 . It is well settled that a gift of immovable property does not come within the purview of section 4 ( 3 )( c ) of Wealth Tax Act . Section 5 ( b ) of that Act provides that if there is no disposition of movable property which can be described as " gifts ", such gift must be deemed to be a gift . If the donor has disposed of only part of the property , then the gift would be exempt from tax . [ 13 D E ; 14 G H ; 15 B ] 3 . The fact that the done e had retained possession and enjoyment of the gifted property will not alter the nature of the gift so long as it is not accepted by the done es . Therefore , the gift cannot be treated as a gift because the done er retain s control over the property . [ 16 F ]

The appellant was appointed as a District and Sessions judge in the State of Orissa . He was posted at Cuttack , on the recommendation of the High Court . On his transfer he joined the new post with effect from October 1 , 1966 . In November 1965 he was transferred to Cuttack where he worked till September 30 , 1967 . On January 31 , 1968 he was promoted as an Additional District Judge . On February 6 , 1969 he was appointed by the Governor of Orissa under Article 233 ( 2 ) of the Constitution for one year . On March 10 , 1970 he was again promoted as Chief Justice of the Orissa High Court and then as Principal Civil Judge , Cuttack . On April 7 , 1971 he was served with a memorandum dated May 9 , 1972 whereby he was asked to submit his explanation within 15 days of the receipt of that memorandum . A copy of the memorandum was forwarded to him . On June 3 , 1973 he submitted another memorandum stating therein that he had been appointed as an additional district judge in view of certain complaints received against him . The Government issued a notification appointing him as a member of the Bar Council of India . By this memorandum the Governor directed that all officers who were holding judicial posts in the state shall be deemed to have retired from service on or after August 1 , 1974 . The appellant challenged the validity of the said order before the High court contending that it was violative of article 235 of the constitution inasmuch as the Governor could not appoint any person as a judge of the Supreme Court unless he was recommended by the High est b ureau cr acy . It was also contended that since the appointment of the appellant as a district judge was made by the President of India under section 14 of the Act , there was no question of consultation with the High Courts . The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant . Allow ing the appeal , ^ HELD : 1 . The power to appoint a district Judge is vested in the Governor under article 234 of the Con stitution . Under article 235 the control over district courts and courts subordinate thereto vests in the High courts . The appellant , a detenu of the Indian Air Force , was detained under section 3 ( 1 ) of the . Act in order to prevent him from acting in any manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order and for preventing his smuggling . He filed an application before the Advisory Board on August 19 , 1955 , against the detention order which was rejected by the Government on September 8 , 1955 . On the same day he made another representation to the State Government that he should be given the grounds of detention along with the grounds but no orders were passed thereon till then . In the meantime , on April 30 , 1956 , the State of Bombay issued a notification under section 10 ( 1 )( b ) of ' the Act rev oking the earlier order of detention dated October 31 , 1956 . The appellant challenged the validity of this order on the ground that it violated article 22 ( 5 ) of Constitution as it infringed the right guaranteed to him under article 21 of the Constitution . Held : ( i ) That the detaining authority had not applied its mind to the existence or otherwise of the legitimate objects of detention and had merely referred to the fact that the petitioner was furnished all the particulars relating to the said grounds of his detention . It is also clear that the detaining authorities did not apply their mind to those facts and mechanically revoked them without applying their mind . ( ii ) The power conferred upon the detaining Authority to act independently of the subjective satisfaction of the detaining officer cannot be held to have been properly exercised because there are no materials on record to show that the relevant material was not considered by the detaining . authority while passing the impugned order .

The appellants , who were the trustees of a temple in question , filed an application before the District Munsif for appointment of their successors as trustees . The trial Judge held that the properties in suit had been granted to them by the erstwhile manager and they were entitled to be appointed as trustees only on the basis of the said order . On appeal , the High Court set aside the decree holding that the alien or was not entitled to any interest in the property and so there could be no question of his being declared a trustee under section 87 of the Act . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that ( 1 ) the original grant made by the then manager of the temple was invalid because it did not confer upon him any title to the property ; ( 2 ) even if he had become a trustee , he would have ceased to be a trustee after the death of the previous manager and therefore , the subsequent removal of the present manager from office amounted to a valid transfer within the meaning of section 88 of the Indian Trusts Act , 1882 ; and ( 3 ) since the original sanction given by the Government to the institution was itself void , the land in dispute vested in the State Government under section 89 A of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act , 1951 , which provided that all rights and interests created by the original trust shall vest in the successor to the person who became the trustee thereof . Held : ( i ) That the original sanctioning authority had jurisdiction to decide whether the lands in dispute belonged to the predecessor of the respondents or not . ( ii ) The original sanction accorded by the Commissioner of Hindu Religious & Charitable Endowments , Madras , was not vitiated by fraud or misrepresentation . It was not open to the Deputy Commissioner to hold that the lands were not transferred to the appellant ' s predecessor . ( iii ) The provisions of sections 87 and 88 of Madras Hindu Public Religious and charitable institutions Act , 1949 , do not apply to the facts of the case .

The appellants were put in possession of the mills and factory on 31 8 1952 . On 12 2 1954 , they became entitled to be paid compensation for the loss sustained by them as a result of the sale of their goods . In pursuance of this agreement , the appellants sold the stocks of raw materials , un finished goods , spare parts etc ., to the respondents who claimed that they had been dispossessed from the premises and that they should be allowed to retain possession thereof . The respondent filed an application under section 7 of the Act claiming that it was not liable to pay any compensation because the property which was the subject matter of the lease was owned by the State Government and therefore the appellants could not claim anything more than what was payable to the Custodian . The trial court dismissed the petition holding that the appellants were not entitled to question the title of the Custodian ి and that the Custodian ' s order was without jurisdiction . The High Court held that the provisions of section 12 ( 1 ) of the Ordinance were not applicable to the case but only to the rights of the appellants . It further held that there was no provision in the Ordinance or in the Rules framed thereunder requiring the Custodian to give notice before taking over possession of any immovable property . Held , that the appeal must fail . Section 12 ( 3 )( c ) of Ordinance No . 43 Of 1949 did not authorise the Custodian , ి to cancel a lease granted by him in favour of the appellant . The effect of the repeal of Ordinance is that the right of the parties to the lease would continue to exist even after the expiry of the period fixed in the lease deed . If the Custodian had taken possession of all the properties belonging to the appellants , he could have done so either by himself or through his agents . The Custodian could not refuse to take possession of those properties unless he gave notice to the other party . The appellants had no legal interest in these properties at all . They were merely lessees and not owners of the same . The proceedings for cancellation of leases are quasi judicial proceedings and cannot be equated with proceedings for determination of rights between the parties .
