The appellant company was a resident of the former Dholpur State in 1947 and had been granted a permit for export of 15 , 000 ma unds . In August 1949 it applied to the Central Government under section 5 ( 2 ) of the Indian Oil Corporation Act , which provided that no person shall sell or offer to sell any oil seeds except under and in accordance with a permit issued by the Central or the Provincial Governments . Under cl . 3 of the agreement the appellant was entitled to receive from the respondent only such quantity of oil as may be determined by the said corporation at the time of granting the permit . Clause 4 of this agreement provided that the appellant would not be liable if he failed to obtain a permit within 12 months from the date of issue of the permit , but if the permit was refused on account of non compliance with the conditions imposed therein , the appellant could have no right to claim refund . On appeal by certificate the High Court held that the agreement did not come within the purview of article VI of the Co ven ant and therefore the appellant ' s application for refund should fail . Held : ( i ) The agreement dated April 1 , 1950 was valid and binding between the parties ; ( ii ) It was not open to the Union of India to make an application for the grant of a permit under the provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act , 1939 , because there was nothing to show that the permission was granted before December 2 , 1947 when the Ordinance came into force . ( iii ) The appellant was not entitled to refund of the amount paid by him after December 2 1947 , because the agreement was not a law . [ 59 B ]

The appellants , a registered dealer under the Madras Commercial Crop s Markets Act , 1939 , were carrying on business in cotton and ground nuts . They sold their goods to dealers at Madurai for sale by them . In order to facilitate the sales of such commodities , they entered into agreements with various dealers for purchase of certain commodities . The transactions were divided between the two companies , one dealing in cotton , another with the object of providing a service to the customers and the other to the traders . The appellants who were dealers in cotton raised disputes about the validity of the provisions of the Madras General Sales Tax Act , 1959 , which provided that no deduction shall be made from the price or commodity agreed upon between the buyer and the seller unless it was shown that there was an agreement between the parties for payment of any amount as compensation or damages payable to the dealer . The question arose whether the appellants were liable to pay tax on the turnover relating to the sale of cotton purchased by them during the relevant period . Held : ( 1 ) that the appellants did not carry on business within the meaning of section 14 of the Act ; ( 2 ) that if the appellants had been paying only a part of the price and paid nothing towards consideration for the use of the premises or services rendered , then the whole of the profit could be taxed under section 14 ; ( 3 ) that even though the transaction was one of sale of goods , the entire profits were attributable to the labour employed therein and therefore the appellants would be liable to tax under the Act .

The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death . His appeal to the High Court failed , but his conviction s were maintained on the ground that there was no evidence to show that he had committed the murder of one person or more than one persons in furtherance of their common intention . Held : ( 1 ) That a sentence of imprisonment for life is an extreme penalty so far as it relates to the crime of murder is concerned ; if two Judges concur in the commission of the offence by the same act , then only this Court can interfere with the discretion of the Judge who has imposed the sentence . In the present case , however , the High Courts have not accepted the verdict of the trial court because they differ ed from the opinion of the two judges regarding the guilt of the accused . There are cases where the High court should be slow to interfere with its judgment and substitute its own discretion for that of the Sessions Judge . But when the High courts come to conclusion that the order of acquittal passed by them was wrong , there is nothing in law which prevents them from doing so . It is well settled that the power of review available to the Supreme Court under article 137 of the Constitution is wide and the very fact that the High C ount has made certain observations against the appellate Judges does not mean that such powers must be exercised sparingly .

The respondents were the legal representatives of one late Raja Vas ired di Chandra Dhar a Prasad , who died on 12th January , 1961 . He had filled up proposal for insurance with the Life Insurance Corporation in respect of his life . The deceased was an employee of the appellant and he submitted to the Life insurance Corporation that the premium payable by him should be paid within three months from the date of death of the assured . On receipt of the said letter , the respondent No . 1 appointed a nominee under the policy as the nominee . The claim made by the widow of the deceased was repudiated by the LIC on the ground that the deceased had not signed any declaration or other document regarding her health at the time of taking the policy . The High Court held that the repudiation was justified because the deceased did not sign the declaration form and therefore there was no concluded contract between the parties . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants : ( i ) that the High Court erred in law in holding that the acceptance must be communicated to the offer er when the application is made ; ( ii ) that since the deceased died before the expiry of the period of three months , the contract could not be completed and hence the contract stood terminated ; and ( iii ) that even if the payment was accepted after the lapse of the stipulated period , the fact that the insured died during the subsistence of the contract would not make the contract void able . Dismis sing the appeals , ^ HELD : 1 . It is well settled that where the terms of a contract are governed by the provisions of another statute which gives effect to the first part of the earlier Act only then it can be taken into consideration for determining whether the later legislation is retrospective or not . [ 10 75 C ] 2 . Held :( i ) The order of a Court is final if it decides some right or liability between the parties in relation to the subject matter of the proceedings before it . In appeal by special leave , HELD : ( i ) Section 19 ( 2 ) is clear that if an allottee has been given a right to be allotted land in the same village or part thereof he shall have preference over others ; but where such right is exercised only after the date mentioned in clause ( d ), then his application would be governed by the provision of section 17 which provides that nothing contained in sections 12 and 19 shall apply to him . In appeal to this Court , HELD : ( i ) The power conferred by the Proviso to Article 309 is of a legislative character and is to be exercised by the Legislature ; its power to amend any part of the Fundamental rules cannot be taken away except by express provision or by necessary intendment . It has been held by this Court that the power to legislate is not an absolute one but is hed ged with limitations . The power to make laws is derived from the Constitution itself and if the legislature by appropriate means makes a law , it can enact a law which comes into force only when it fram es the law and the procedure for doing so must have some effect . No . 36 dated April 29 , 1969 is invalid . The said amendments are beyond the scope of the enabling power conferred on the Government by section 55 of the Act . [ 593 D B ] ( iv ) The amendment made by G , O . M . No , 35 dated March 28 , 1983 is also bad because it violates Articles 14 and 21 of the constitution inasmuch as it does not take away the right conferred by Article 309 of the Con sti t ution to the executive . The respondents were registered dealers under the Bombay Sales Tax Act . They claimed exemption from sales tax on a taxable turnover including purchases of goods sold by them to their buyers in West Bengal , but they continued to be the owners of the goods till the goods had crossed the customs barrier and thus entered the export stream and so no tax was real isable on these sales . On the question whether the sale made by the appellant to purchasers who are not registered dealers is liable to be taxed as " sales of goods ", HELD : ( 1 ) The words " a person " in section 10 ( b ) mean a registered dealer and not an unregistered dealer . [ 11 B ] ( 2 ) The word " a " used in section 8 ( b ), must be given its natural meaning without any doubt or ambiguity . It does not mean that all sales effected by a registered assessee should be subjected to tax irrespective of the fact whether such sales have taken place within the State of Bombay or outside it . If the intention of the Legislature was to levy purchase tax only if the goods were actually despatched outside the State , then there would be no need for making a declaration of intention to sell the goods at all . [ 12 G H ; 13 A C ] ( 3 ) In order to make the declaration of the intention clear , it has to be shown that the goods which were actually delivered were intended to be purchased by the purchasing dealer himself . There is nothing in the language of the section which requires that the declaration should be made before the delivery of the certificate . The purpose of the declaration contemplated by the section is to enable the purchaser to obtain the benefit of the exemption provided by the notification . When he sells the goods to another person , he becomes the owner thereof . He may not be aware of the actual transaction of the sale . But when he sells his goods to others , he is not a registered purchaser because the goods are not available to him . Therefore , the use of the words " one who is not registered dealer " in clause ( b ). of the Explanation to section 10 cannot be said to be a deliberate act with the intention to evade payment of tax . [ 14 D E ]

The appellant , a tenant of the premises in dispute , was an occupant of certain premises . Held : ( 1 ) that section 4 of the Rent Control Act does not provide for a machinery for recovery of the amount which is recoverable under the provisions relating to eviction of tenants ; it only provides for a procedure for recovery thereof . If the landlord has been given a remedy by way of execution or otherwise , then the remedy provided under the Code of Civil Procedure is by implication barred . ( 2 ) Section 10 ( 1 )( vii ) of the Act does provide for the recovery of possession of the property by the landlord either by himself or through his successor in interest . It does not create a new cause of action so as to give rise to a fresh cause of actions . ( 3 ) The words " subject to the provisions regarding jurisdiction of Courts " in section 4 are wide enough to include within its ambit all questions of title arising out of the provisions about the proper rent payable by the tenant to the landlord . ( 4 ) The expression " subject matter of the present proceedings " used in section 10 ( 2 )( vi ) means the entire proceeding before the Rent Controller and the appellate authority and therefore the word " subject " occurring in section 11 would be limited to those matters where the original order passed by the Rent contro ller is set aside by the Appellate Authority and the matter is remanded back to him for passing a fresh order after hearing both sides .

The Assistant Collector rejected the claim on the ground that the goods had been supplied by the buyer to the appellant without any contract between the parties or even with an intention to evade payment of duty . The petitioner was convicted for an offence under section 630 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs . 1 , 000 / with default stipulation . He filed a revision petition before the High Court against his conviction and sentence . The High Court dismissed his revision application holding that he had no jurisdiction to entertain it as the provisions of section 630 ( l )( b ) were not applicable in view of the fact that the term ' officer or employee ' used in sub section ( 1 ) of section 631 did not include any past officer or employees of a company . Dismis sing the special leave petition , ^ HELD : ( i ) Section 630 ( 1 )( b ), which is similar to section 630 , does not contain any limitation on the power of the court to grant relief from liability for wrongful withholding of property . It only provides that where such property has been wrongfully withheld by the accused person , the court may direct payment of such amount to him . In this case , there was no express provision empowering the court either to order payment of compensation or to make restitution of the property . [ 10 31 C ] ( ii ) The expression " any such property of a Company " occurring in sub sec .( 1 ) must be construed to mean " every property of the company ". The word " any " in cl . ( b ) of s . 630 ( I ) would refer only to existing officers or employees who are entitled to receive the property of that company . [ 11 31 B E ] ( iii ) The words " any property of any company " appearing in cl .( b ) must necessarily include all assets attached to the undertaking . If the intention of the legislature was to exclude the operation of the clause ( c ) of sub section 2 of section 629 of the Act , then the use of the words " other than those specified in clauses ( a ) and ( b )" in the proviso to sub section 3 of section 5 will have to be given effect to . [ 12 31 D F ] ( iv ) The language of the section is clear and unambiguous . There is nothing in the context to indicate that the Legislature intended to give a restricted meaning to the words ' any property '. The words ' other than any such land or building ' do not cover the present cases . [ 32 G H ; 33 A B ]

He had been appointed as an Arch aka by the f ounder , and continued to be so till his death on January 16 , 1954 . On the death of Shri Vithal she became entitled to all the properties and assets belonging to the deity . She died on February 17 , 1955 leaving behind her two sons , namely , ( 1 ) Shri Vithal s / o Gopal das ji , ( 2 ) Shri Shankar lal Moti ram ji , and ( 3 ) Shri B . N . Gang uli , who was also the f oun ders of the Hindu public . In 1946 , the f akir s of the deity installed in the temple were removed from the temple . A suit for declaration that the temple was not a public temple was filed in the Court of the Assistant Charity Commissioner . The appellant contended that the idol was private and that the deity was a public trust within the meaning of section 2 ( 13 ) of the Act . The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal preferred by the respondents holding that the institution was a private temple and that it was not open to the appellant to challenge the validity of the order passed by the Assistant Commissioner under section 18 ( 1 ). It further held that the appellant ' s claim that the property belonged to him was not established beyond doubt . Allow ing the appeal , HELD : ( i ) The deity installed at the temple is a public religious endowment within the definition of section 3 ( 14 ) of Bombay Public Trust Act , 1950 . [ 531 C ] ( ii ) The expression " public " used in section 2 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act , 1951 must receive a restricted meaning unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context . The word " public ", according to common usage , would include even management of property by the State . [ 532 D E ] ( iii ) The words " any interest in land " occurring in section 11 ( 6 ) of this Act are wide enough to cover every kind of property including money , present or future , held by the public as such . The expression ' immovable property ' has no fixed connotation . It means movable property or immovable property or personal rights or interests therein . The appellant company was assessed to income tax for the year 1943 44 . In a writ petition filed by it under article 226 of the Constitution , the High Court quashed the assessment on the ground that there had been no reasonable basis for the levy and collection of income tax in respect of the period between January 1 , 1946 , to March 31 , 1947 . On appeal by special leave , Held : ( i ) The power conferred upon the Income Tax Officer by section 13 ( 3 ) of the Act is not an un guided power but only one of the several circumstances which would justify the imposition of penalty ; ( ii ) the order passed by the Income tax officer must be based on relevant material and should not be arbitrary or unreasonable ; ( iii ) the power conferred by section 15 of the Central Provinces and Ber ar Sales Tax Act , 1947 , is not a judicial power and therefore cannot be exercised arbitrarily ; ( iv ) the fact that the assessee has paid up the amount due from him does not mean that he is entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 14 of the Bombay General Clauses Act , 19 04 ; ( v ) the notice issued by the assessing authority under section 13 of the , is invalid because it did not give any opportunity to the assessee to make his representation against the proposed demand ; ( vi ) the proceedings taken by the taxing authorities are quasi criminal in character and do not affect the validity of the notice served on the assessee ; ( vii ) the notices issued by them were valid as they were made after the expiry of three years from the end of the year in question and were therefore valid ; ( viii ) the orders of assessment were void and illegal inasmuch as they imposed unreasonable restrictions on the right of the assessees to carry on business in their premises without complying with the requirements of sections 4 and 5 of the Ordinance ; ( ix ) the assessments were made ex parte without affording any opportunity of being heard to the appellants ; ( x ) the assessment orders were bad as they had been passed without giving any opportunity and without hearing to the petitioners ; ( xi ) the procedure prescribed by law was not followed in making the assessment ; ( xii ) the impugned notices were barred by time since the assessment order was made beyond six months from the date of the last notice dated December 29 , 1955 ; ( xiii ) the High court erred in holding that the first respondent could have no jurisdiction to issue the said notices ; ( xiv ) the second contention urged by the respondents was well founded ; ( xv ) the third contention was also rejected

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1956 . It had a factory at A lex andra , and it carried on its business from that place to its head office situated at Bombay . In 1959 , the Company entered into an agreement with the Government of India for the sale of certain machinery including the machinery installed by the Company . Under this agreement the Company agreed to sell all its assets and liabilities to the purchasers subject to the terms and conditions set out therein . Clause ( 2 ) of the agreement provided that the purchaser shall not be entitled to any compensation or damages against the Company if the Company failed to carry out the terms of the contract within 30 days after the expiry of the period mentioned in clause ( 1 ). The Company did not pay any compensation as required under cl s . ( 3 ), ( 4 ) and ( 5 ) of Art . III of the Agreement . On December 15 , 1953 , the Union served a notice upon the Company calling upon it to show cause why the amount should not be recovered from it . The Company replied contending that the Company was liable to pay the amount due to it . By a letter dated January 19 , 1955 , the President of the Company informed the Company that the amount would be paid only after the termination of the agency and that the payment would be made after the expiration of the term of the Agency . The company also stated that the amounts were payable only after termination of agency and therefore there was no question of any claim being barred by limitation . The Tribunal held that the Union was not entitled to recover the amount because the Union had not been able to establish that the workmen were entitled to receive the amount . The High Court dismissed the petition . Held : ( i ) The liability to pay compensation arises when the services are terminated before the expiry or termination of service ; but where the services have been terminated without giving one month ' s notice or wages in lieu thereof , the liability is attracted by the fact that the employment has continued till the termination thereof . The High Court dismissed the revision petition filed by the tenant holding that since the premises were let out at a monthly rent of Rs . 500 /- it was not open to the landlord to evict the tenant from the said premises without complying with the provisions of Section 20 ( 1 ) of the Act . Hence this appeal by special leave . Allow ing the appeal , ^ HELD : 1 . 1 The provision contained in sub section 2 clause ( 2 ) of Section 2 is clear that if the provisions contained in Section 20 are not complied with the right of the tenant to obtain possession of the building shall not be available to him . The Calcutta Thi ka Tenancy ( Amendment ) Act , 1953 was passed by the West Bengal Legislature in 1949 . Section 4 of the Act provided that notwithstanding anything contained in any law or contract , no suit shall be instituted against a tenant for his eviction from any land held by him as a th ika tenant except on one or more of the following grounds : ( 1 ) that he required the land for personal cultivation ; ( 2 ) that the landlord required the premises reasonably and bonafide for occupation by himself or any member of his family dependent on him ; and ( 3 ) that there was no other suitable accommodation available to him for the purpose . In the meantime section 5 of the Ordinance of 1952 which came into force on February 28 , 1949 , was amended by adding two more sections with retrospective effect . By this amendment the word ' th ika ' was substituted for the words ' th hik an ' instead of ' th ik '. The appellant filed a written statement before the Subordinate Judge denying the claim made by the respondent . He also contended that the tenancy had been created prior to the coming into force of the West Punjab Premises Tenancy ( Second Amendment ) Ordinance , 1952 but it could not therefore be said that the provisions of the Amending Act were applicable to the present case . Held , that the question whether the provisions relating to th ika tenants were applicable only to suits and appeals pending on January 31 , 1951 did not arise at all because the amending Act of 1953 was not retrospective in operation . It was well settled that where a statute is prospective unless it is expressly or by necessary implication made retrospective either expressly or impliedly its retrospective operation may be implied if the legislative intent is clearly to give retrospective operation to a statute so as to take away or impair an existing right .

The High Court of Allahabad , by its judgment dated November 6 , 1985 in Writ Petition No . 42 11 / 83 directed the State Government to pay to the petitioner a higher scale with effect from January 1 , 1986 and also for similar duties as were paid to Bench Secretaries Grade I . In pursuance thereof , the State of Uttar Pradesh issued an order on February 9 , 1988 whereby it fixed the pay scales of different categories of posts at Rs . 200 450 and Rs . 5 15 715 respectively . On March 31 , 1989 , the Government appointed a Pay Commission to examine the question of parity between two sets of employees who had been working in the same cadre . The Committee submitted its report on April 25 , 1990 recommending that all the three pay scales should be revised to Rs . 150 350 ( pre revised ) with effect form June 1 , 1987 . The recommendations of the Committee were accepted by the Government . However , the pay scale was not revised to the post of Bench Secretary . The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the said recommendation contending that since the decision of the Government was based on no principle or without any rational basis , there could be no revision of pay scales . The High court dismissed the writ petition holding that the decision taken by the committee was fair and reasonable and did not call for interference . Hence this appeal by special leave . Allow ing the appeal , this Court , HELD : 1 . The fixation of pay under the Rules is a matter of policy . It has a rational nexus with the object to be sought for , as stated earlier , which is to promote the welfare of the public . [ 227 C ] 2 . The pay structure of the various categories of employees are determined by the rules framed by the Chief Justice of the High court . Therefore , the Chief justice cannot sit in judgment over the decision arrived at by the Committee . [ 228 E F ] 3 . The power conferred upon the Chief Judge under Article 235 of the Constitution is a legislative function . He can only act in accordance with law . If he finds that the Chief Minister ' s view is not correct then the Chief Ministers decision must be final . [ 230 D ] 5 . The appellant , a Government Company incorporated under the Companies Act , was constituted under section 65 of the Madhya Pradesh Nagar T atha Gram Niv esh Adhiniyam 1973 . Section 64 provided that subject to any general or special order which the State Government may make in this behalf , it shall be lawful for the State government to declare by notification in the official Gazette that no tax shall be levied on building materials and plant ations used exclusively for agricultural purposes from such date as may be specified in the notification . Under section 68 ( 1 ) every owner of land within the area of a municipality is required to give notice of his intention to impose property tax . Section 69 provides that where any person fails to pay the tax due within the time fixed by the notice he shall be liable to pay interest at the rate of two per cent per month on the amount of tax remaining unpaid from the day immediately following the said date till the payment thereof . In the present case , there were certain dues payable by respondent 1 to the appellant company . On March 31 , 1976 , the appellant filed an application before the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution praying for quashing of the demand made by the State . The High Court dismissed the petition holding that since the liability to pay tax had been created by the Central Act , the State Legislature could not have enacted the impugned law . There is nothing in the language of the enactment which de bars the State legislature from doing so . [ 63 E F ] 3 . The appellant , a lessee of the Rajah for five years from January 10 , 1942 to December 10 , 1947 applied to the Collector for confirmation of his lease under r . 47 ( 1 ) of the Mineral Concession Rules , 1949 , and that he was informed by the Government that the lease had been determined on February 12 , 1952 . On March 15 , 1953 , the appellant filed an application before the Board of Revenue for confirmation and for grant of a fresh lease in respect of certain lands which were leased out to him . The Board rejected the application holding that it did not contain any terms or conditions relating to the renewal of the lease . In appeal to this Court , HELD : ( i ) The second proviso to rule 47 ( 3 ) does not deal with the question as to whether the lease granted by the previous owner is renewed or not ; but only provides that such renew als shall be subject to the same conditions as are laid down in the first proviso to s . 20 ( 1 ). [ 49 B ] ( ii ) Rule 47 ( 2 )( b ) deals with the termination of rights created after July 1 , 1945 , one would have expected those conditions to be mentioned in the second proviso itself . But if the third proviso applies to rights created before July 1 . 1945 , all right created after that date must also fall with it . It cannot therefore be said that the third condition has no bearing on the validity of the second Proviso because it merely says that the leases will be renewed for a period exceeding one year . If the third Proviso comes into operation , there can be no doubt that the Government should have accepted the contention put forward by the appellant . [ 50 D E ]
